children: Uganda is positioning its first crude exports for Asian markets as the country moves into the final commercial phase of its long-awaited oil project, with global energy trader Vitol appointed to market and sell the crude internationally from early 2027.

The appointment, formally announced on September 7, comes days after Uganda unveiled the name of its export crude, Pearl Sweet—a medium-to-heavy, low-sulphur crude with a high conversion yield that officials say is well suited to refiners seeking relatively low-cost feedstock for producing compliant fuels.“Pearl Sweet is well suited to many Asian refineries, and we anticipate a great deal of interest,” said Kieran Gallagher, head of Vitol Asia.

The appointment marks a major step for Uganda, more than two decades after commercial oil was discovered in the Albertine Graben. In a joint statement, the Uganda National Oil Company (Unoc) and the Ministry of Energy said Pearl Sweet would be available for export from early 2027 as the government and its partners complete production and export infrastructure.

Uganda expects to produce up to 230,000 barrels of crude oil per day from the Tilenga and Kingfisher development areas. The crude will be transported through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (Eacop) to the export terminal at Tanzania’s port of Tanga, from where it will be shipped to international markets.“Vitol’s appointment is another sign that Uganda is moving from development to delivery. As we complete the production and export infrastructure, we are now putting in place the commercial capability to take Pearl Sweet to the world,” said Energy minister Dr Monica Musenero.
She said Vitol’s global reach, trading expertise and logistics capabilities would be critical in matching Uganda’s crude with suitable refiners and maximising the value of the country’s oil exports.
The focus on Asia is also consistent with Uganda’s broader strategy to develop Tanga into a regional energy and logistics hub.

On August 6, Unoc, Vitol and the Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) signed an agreement to develop an energy hub at the Port of Tanga, which is strategically positioned to serve markets in Asia and the Middle East while providing an additional logistics corridor for landlocked Uganda and neighbouring countries.

Vitol has already been working with Unoc on Uganda’s petroleum-products supply arrangements since last year. The companies have also signed a $2 billion financing facility to support the development of energy infrastructure.
The start of crude exports in early 2027 would bring Uganda’s oil ambitions into their first major commercial phase, although government revenue expectations have become more conservative.

Meanwhile, Uganda’s two upstream projects are moving closer to first oil. The 40,000-barrel-per-day Kingfisher project, operated by CNOOC Uganda, reached mechanical completion on August 24, according to CNOOC Uganda president Dr Liu Xiangdong. The larger 190,000-barrel-per-day Tilenga project, operated by TotalEnergies, is also advancing towards production.
The 1,443-kilometre Eacop, which will carry Uganda’s crude from Hoima to Tanga, is 92.7 per cent complete, according to the latest contractor and government figures.

With production facilities nearing completion, the pipeline approaching the finish line, and Vitol now tasked with finding buyers, Uganda’s oil project is moving from construction to the test that matters most: turning its first barrels into export revenue.
